{{Short description|Mathematical group}}
{{for|finite groups with all characteristic abelian subgroups cyclic|group of symplectic type}}
{{Lie groups |Classical}}
{{Group theory sidebar |Topological}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''symplectic group''' is the [[group (mathematics)|group]] of [[linear transformation]]s that preserve the geometric structure of [[phase space]], the space of position and momentum variables used in [[classical mechanics]]. It is defined as the group of linear changes of coordinates on phase space that preserve the [[symplectic vector space|symplectic form]].

The symplectic groups are usually denoted <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math>, where <math>n</math> is a positive integer and <math>\mathbb{F}</math> is a [[field (mathematics)|field]], often the [[real number]]s or [[complex number]]s. They are among the four families of [[classical group]]s and play a central role in [[symplectic geometry]], [[Hamiltonian mechanics]], and [[representation theory]]. A related but different family is the '''compact symplectic group''', usually denoted <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> or <math>\mathrm{USp}(n)</math>.

== Terminology and notation ==
The name "symplectic" was introduced by [[Hermann Weyl]] as a replacement for older terminology such as '''line complex group'''. It was intended as a Greek-based analogue of the word "[[complex number|complex]]".

The notation <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> usually denotes the symplectic group of a <math>2n</math>-dimensional symplectic vector space over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>\mathbb{F}</math>. A related but different family is the '''compact symplectic group''', denoted <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> or <math>\mathrm{USp}(n)</math>, which is the compact real form of the complex symplectic group.

Many authors use slightly different notations, often differing by factors of <math>2</math>. In [[Élie Cartan|Cartan]]'s classification, the Lie algebra of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math> has type <math>C_n</math>.

=={{math|Sp(2''n'', '''F''')}}==
The symplectic group is a [[classical group]] defined as the set of [[linear transformations]] of a <math>2n</math>-dimensional [[vector space]] over the field <math>\mathbb{F}</math> which preserve a [[nondegenerate form|non-degenerate]] [[skew-symmetric matrix|skew-symmetric]] [[bilinear form]]. Such a vector space is called a [[symplectic vector space]], and the symplectic group of an abstract symplectic vector space <math>V</math> is denoted <math>\operatorname{Sp}(V)</math>. Upon fixing a basis for <math>V</math>, the symplectic form is represented by a [[nonsingular matrix|nonsingular]] skew-symmetric matrix <math>J</math>, and <math>\operatorname{Sp}(V)</math> is identified with the group of <math>2n\times 2n</math> matrices over <math>\mathbb{F}</math> satisfying

<math display="block">\{M \in M_{2n\times 2n}(\mathbb{F}) : M^\mathrm{T} J M = J\}.</math>

This matrix group is denoted <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> or <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n,\mathbb{F})</math>, although the notation depends on the convention being used. Here <math>M^T</math> denotes the [[transpose]] of <math>M</math>.

In an arbitrary basis, the matrix <math>J</math> need not have any particular form. However, one can choose a ''symplectic basis'', in which the form is represented by the standard matrix

<math display="block">\Omega = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_n \\ -I_n & 0 \end{pmatrix},</math>

where <math>I_n</math> is the identity matrix. In such a basis,

<math display="block">\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})=\{M\in M_{2n\times 2n}(\mathbb{F}):M^\mathrm{T}\Omega M=\Omega\}.</math>

In this case, <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> can be expressed as those block matrices <math>(\begin{smallmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{smallmatrix})</math>, where <math>A, B, C, D \in M_{n \times n}(\mathbb{F})</math>, satisfying the three equations:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
-C^\mathrm{T}A + A^\mathrm{T}C &= 0, \\
-C^\mathrm{T}B + A^\mathrm{T}D &= I_n, \\
-D^\mathrm{T}B + B^\mathrm{T}D &= 0.
\end{align}</math>

Since all symplectic matrices have [[determinant]] <math>1</math>, the symplectic group is a [[subgroup]] of the [[special linear group]] <math>\operatorname{SL}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math>. When <math>n=1</math>, the symplectic condition on a matrix is satisfied [[if and only if]] the determinant is one, so that <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2,\mathbb{F})=\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb{F})</math>. For <math>n>1</math>, there are additional conditions, i.e. <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> is then a proper subgroup of <math>\operatorname{SL}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math>.

Typically, the field <math>\mathbb{F}</math> is the field of [[real number]]s <math>\mathbb{R}</math> or [[complex number]]s <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. In these cases <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> is a real or complex [[Lie group]] of real or complex dimension <math>n(2n+1)</math>, respectively. These groups are [[connected space|connected]] but [[Compact group|non-compact]].

The [[Center (group theory)|center]] of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> consists of the matrices <math>I_{2n}</math> and <math>-I_{2n}</math> as long as the [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic of the field]] is not <math>2</math>.<ref>[http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Symplectic_group "Symplectic group"], ''[[Encyclopedia of Mathematics]]'' Retrieved on 13 December 2014.</ref> Since the center of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> is discrete and its quotient modulo the center is a [[simple group]], <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> is considered a [[Simple Lie group#Comments on the definition|simple Lie group]].

The real rank of the corresponding Lie algebra, and hence of the Lie group <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math>, is <math>n</math>.

The [[Lie algebra]] of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> is the set

<math display="block">\mathfrak{sp}(2n,F) = \{X \in M_{2n \times 2n}(F) : \Omega X + X^\mathrm{T} \Omega = 0\},</math>

equipped with the [[Commutator#Ring theory|commutator]] as its Lie bracket.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Prop. 3.25</ref> For the standard skew-symmetric bilinear form <math>\Omega = (\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & I \\ -I & 0 \end{smallmatrix})</math>, this Lie algebra is the set of all block matrices <math>(\begin{smallmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{smallmatrix})</math> subject to the conditions

:<math>\begin{align}
A &= -D^\mathrm{T}, \\
B &= B^\mathrm{T}, \\
C &= C^\mathrm{T}.
\end{align}</math>

==={{math|Sp(2''n'', '''C''')}}===
The symplectic group over the field of complex numbers is a [[Compact group|non-compact]], [[simply connected]], [[simple Lie group]]. The definition of this group includes ''no'' conjugates (contrary to what one might naively expect) but instead it is exactly the same as the definition bar the field change.{{sfn|Hall|2015|p=10}}

==={{math|Sp(2''n'', '''R''')}}===
<math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> is a real, non-compact, connected simple Lie group of dimension <math>n(2n+1)</math>.<ref name="Knapp2002" />
It has fundamental group isomorphic to the integers under addition.{{sfn|Hall|2015}}
As the real form of a simple complex Lie algebra, its Lie algebra is the split real form of <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math>.<ref name="Knapp2002">{{cite book
 |last=Knapp
 |first=Anthony W.
 |title=Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction
 |edition=2nd
 |publisher=Birkhäuser
 |year=2002
}}</ref>

The exponential map from <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> to <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> is not surjective.<ref name="Djokovic1980">{{cite journal
 |last=Djoković
 |first=Dragomir Ž.
 |title=On the exponential map in classical Lie groups
 |journal=Journal of Algebra
 |volume=64
 |issue=1
 |year=1980
 |pages=76–88
}}</ref>

For every <math>S</math> in <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math>, one has a Cartan/polar decomposition<ref name="Knapp2002" /><ref name="Benoist2023">{{cite arXiv
 |last=Benoist
 |first=Yves
 |title=On the rational symplectic group
 |eprint=2208.02549
 |class=math.GR
 |year=2023
}}</ref>
<math display="block">S = OZO'</math>
with <math>O,O' \in \operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})\cap\operatorname{SO}(2n)\cong\operatorname{U}(n)</math>
and <math>Z=\begin{pmatrix}D&0\\0&D^{-1}\end{pmatrix}</math>.
As a manifold, <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> is diffeomorphic to <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> times a vector space of dimension <math>n(n+1)</math>.<ref name="Knapp2002" />

===Generators===
====Infinitesimal generators====
The members of the symplectic Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> are the [[Hamiltonian matrix|Hamiltonian matrices]].

These are matrices, <math>Q</math> such that
<math display="block">Q = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & -A^\mathrm{T} \end{pmatrix}</math>
where <math>B</math> and <math>C</math> are [[Symmetric matrix|symmetric matrices]]. See [[classical group]] for a derivation.

====Generation by transvections====
The symplectic group is generated by its symplectic [[shear mapping|transvection]]s. More precisely, if <math>(V,J)</math> is a finite-dimensional symplectic vector space over <math>\mathbb{F}</math>, then <math>{\mathrm{Sp}(V,\omega)}</math> is generated by the transformations
<math display="block">T_{v,\lambda}(x)=x+\lambda\,(x^TJv)\,v,</math>
where <math>v\in V</math> and <math>\lambda\in\mathbb{F}</math>. This is a general part of the structure theory of the classical groups, and appears in early form in work of Dieudonné; see also later treatments devoted specifically to symplectic transvections and the subgroups they generate.<ref name=Dieudonne1955>{{cite journal
 |last=Dieudonné
 |first=Jean
 |title=Sur les générateurs des groupes classiques
 |journal=Summa Brasiliensis Mathematicae
 |volume=3
 |year=1955
 |pages=149–179
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Brown
 |first1=Ronald
 |last2=Humphries
 |first2=Stephen P.
 |title=Orbits under symplectic transvections. I
 |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society
 |series=3
 |volume=52
 |issue=3
 |year=1986
 |pages=517–531
 |doi=10.1112/plms/s3-52.3.517
}}</ref>

====Generation by involutions====
The symplectic group <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math> can be generated by linear transformations <math>A:V\to V</math> of the symplectic vector space <math>(V,J)</math> such that <math>A^2 = I</math> and <math>A^TJA = -J</math>.<ref name="Dieudonne1955" /><ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Wonenburger
 |first=Anna
 |title=Transformations which are products of two involutions
 |journal=Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics
 |volume=16
 |issue=4
 |year=1966
 |pages=327–338
}}</ref>

===Example of symplectic matrices===
For <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})</math>, the group of <math>2\times 2</math> matrices with determinant <math>1</math>, the three symplectic <math>(0,1)</math>-matrices are:<ref>[http://mathworld.wolfram.com/SymplecticGroup.html Symplectic Group], (source: [[Wolfram MathWorld]]), downloaded February 14, 2012</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},\quad \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\quad \text{and} \quad
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. </math>

==== Sp(2n, R) ====
It turns out that <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> can have a fairly explicit description using generators. If we let <math>\operatorname{Sym}(n)</math> denote the symmetric <math>n\times n</math> matrices, then <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> is generated by <math>D(n)\cup N(n) \cup \{\Omega\},</math> where
<math display="block">\begin{align}
D(n) &= \left\{ \left. \begin{bmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & (A^T)^{-1} \end{bmatrix} \,\right| \, A \in \operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{R})
\right\} \\[6pt]
N(n) &= \left\{ \left. \begin{bmatrix} I_n & B \\ 0 & I_n \end{bmatrix} \, \right| \, B \in \operatorname{Sym}(n)\right\}
\end{align}</math>
are subgroups of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|first1=Gerald B. |last1=Folland|title=Harmonic analysis in phase space|date=2016|publisher=Princeton Univ Press|isbn=978-1-4008-8242-7|location=Princeton|page=173|oclc=945482850}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Habermann |first1=Katharina |title=Introduction to symplectic Dirac operators|date=2006|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-540-33421-7|oclc=262692314|page=2}}</ref>

===Relationship with symplectic geometry===
[[Symplectic geometry]] is the study of [[symplectic manifold]]s. The [[tangent space]] at any point on a symplectic manifold is a [[symplectic vector space]].<ref>[https://empg.maths.ed.ac.uk/Activities/BRST/ "Lecture Notes – Lecture 2: Symplectic reduction"], Retrieved on 30 January 2015.</ref> As noted earlier, structure preserving transformations of a symplectic vector space form a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] and this group is <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{F})</math>, depending on the dimension of the space and the [[Field (mathematics)|field]] over which it is defined.

A symplectic vector space is itself a symplectic manifold. A transformation under an [[Group action (mathematics)|action]] of the symplectic group is thus, in a sense, a linearised version of a [[symplectomorphism]] which is a more general structure preserving transformation on a symplectic manifold.

=={{math|Sp(''n'')}}==

The '''compact symplectic group'''<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Section 1.2.8</ref> <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> is the intersection of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math> with the <math>2n\times 2n</math> unitary group:

:<math>\operatorname{Sp}(n):=\operatorname{Sp}(2n;\mathbb{C})\cap\operatorname{U}(2n)=\operatorname{Sp}(2n;\mathbb{C})\cap\operatorname {SU} (2n).</math>

It is sometimes written as <math>\operatorname{USp}(2n)</math>. Alternatively, <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> can be described as the subgroup of <math>\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{H})</math> (invertible [[quaternion]]ic matrices) that preserves the standard [[hermitian form]] on <math>\mathbb{H}^n</math>:

:<math>\langle x, y\rangle = \bar x_1 y_1 + \cdots + \bar x_n y_n.</math>

That is, <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> is just the [[Classical group#Sp(p, q) – the quaternionic unitary group|quaternionic unitary group]], <math>\operatorname{U}(n,\mathbb{H})</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} p. 14</ref> Indeed, it is sometimes called the '''hyperunitary group'''. Also <math>\operatorname{Sp}(1)</math> is the group of quaternions of norm <math>1</math>, equivalent to {{math|[[SU(2)]]}} and topologically a [[3-sphere|{{math|3}}-sphere]] <math>\mathcal{S}^3</math>.

Note that <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> is ''not'' a symplectic group in the sense of the previous section&mdash;it does not preserve a non-degenerate skew-symmetric <math>\mathbb{H}</math>-bilinear form on <math>\mathbb{H}^n</math>: there is no such form except the zero form. Rather, it is isomorphic to a subgroup of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math>, and so does preserve a complex [[symplectic manifold|symplectic form]] in a vector space of twice the dimension. As explained below, the Lie algebra of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> is the compact [[real form]] of the complex symplectic Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math>.

<math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> is a real Lie group with (real) dimension <math>n(2n+1)</math>. It is [[Compact space|compact]] and [[simply connected]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Prop. 13.12</ref>

The Lie algebra of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> is given by the quaternionic [[skew-Hermitian]] matrices, the set of <math>n\times n</math> quaternionic matrices that satisfy

:<math>A+A^{\dagger} = 0</math>

where <math>A^{\dagger}</math> is the [[conjugate transpose]] of <math>A</math> (here one takes the quaternionic conjugate). The Lie bracket is given by the commutator.

===Important subgroups===
Some main subgroups are:

: <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n) \supset \operatorname{Sp}(n-1)</math>
: <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n) \supset \operatorname{U}(n) </math>
: <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2) \supset \operatorname{O}(4)</math>

Conversely it is itself a subgroup of some other groups:

: <math>\operatorname{SU}(2n) \supset \operatorname{Sp}(n)</math>
: <math>\operatorname{F}_4 \supset \operatorname{Sp}(4)</math>
: <math>\operatorname{G}_2 \supset \operatorname{Sp}(1)</math>

There are also the [[isomorphism]]s of the [[Lie algebras]] <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2)=\mathfrak{so}(5)</math> and <math>\mathfrak{sp}(1)=\mathfrak{so}(3)=\mathfrak{su}(2)</math>.

The unitary symplectic group <math>\operatorname{USp}(n)</math> can be represented in terms of a [[Clifford algebra]] defined as a [[Tensor product of algebras|tensor product]] of quaternion algebras called hyperquaternion numbers. One has, <math>\mathbb{H}^{\otimes 2}=\mathbb{H}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{H}=M_{4\times 4}(\mathbb{R})= Cl_{3,1}\mathbb{(R)}</math>. Hence, <math>\mathbb{H}^{\otimes 3}=M_{4\times 4}(\mathbb{H})</math> entails the compact symplectic group <math>\operatorname{USp}(4)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Girard |first1=P.R. |last2=Clarysse |first2=P. |last3=Pujol |first3=R. |last4=Delachartre |first4=P. |date=2025 |title=Hyperquaternionic unitary symplectic groups: A unifying tool for physics|url=https://rdcu.be/exfs2 |journal=Advances in Applied Clifford Algebras |volume=35 |issue=40 |publisher= Springer |pages= |jstor= |doi=10.1007/s00006-025-01402-w |access-date=}}</ref>

=={{math|Sp(2''n'', '''Z''')}}==
The integral symplectic group <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z})</math> is the subgroup of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> consisting of matrices with integer entries. Equivalently, it is the group of <math>2n\times 2n</math> integer matrices preserving the standard symplectic form:
:<math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z})=\{M\in M_{2n}(\mathbb{Z}): M^\mathrm{T}JM=J\},</math>
where
:<math>J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}.</math>
For <math>n=1</math>, this group coincides with the [[modular group]] <math>\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})</math>.

The group <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z})</math> acts on the [[Siegel upper half-space]], the space of symmetric complex <math>n\times n</math> matrices with positive-definite imaginary part, by fractional linear transformations
:<math>\gamma\cdot\tau=(A\tau+B)(C\tau+D)^{-1}, \qquad
\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\in \operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z}).</math>
For this reason, <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z})</math> is also called the [[Siegel modular group]] of degree <math>n</math>.

Its [[congruence subgroup]]s, such as the principal congruence subgroup
:<math>\Gamma_n(m)=\{\gamma\in\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z}): \gamma\equiv I_{2n}\pmod m\},</math>
play a central role in the theory of [[Siegel modular form]]s. The quotient of Siegel upper half-space by <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{Z})</math> is the moduli space of [[principally polarized abelian variety|principally polarized abelian varieties]] of dimension <math>n</math>, and quotients by congruence subgroups correspond to adding level structure.

Other [[arithmetic subgroup]]s of the symplectic group, such as [[paramodular group]]s are also studied in arithmetic geometry.

==Relationship between the symplectic groups==
Every complex, [[semisimple Lie algebra]] has a [[Real form (Lie theory)#Split real form|split real form]] and a [[Real form (Lie theory)#Compact real form|compact real form]]; the former is called a [[complexification]] of the latter two.

The Lie algebra of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math> is [[Semisimple Lie algebra|semisimple]] and is denoted <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{C})</math>. Its [[Real form (Lie theory)#Split real form|split real form]] is <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> and its [[Real form (Lie theory)#Compact real form|compact real form]] is <math>\mathfrak{sp}(n)</math>. These correspond to the Lie groups <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> and <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math> respectively.

The algebras, <math>\mathfrak{sp}(p,n-p)</math>, which are the Lie algebras of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(p,n-p)</math>, are the [[Metric signature|indefinite signature]] equivalent to the compact form.
===Accidental isomorphisms===
A number of [[exceptional isomorphisms of classical groups|accidental isomorphisms]] also exist, with various [[spin group]]s:
* <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2,\mathbb{F})\cong\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb{F})</math> (in characteristic different from two), and <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})\cong\operatorname{Spin}_0(1,2)</math>. This is because the special linear group automatically preserves any symplectic form in two dimensions.
* <math>\operatorname{Sp}(1)\cong\operatorname{SU}(2)\cong\operatorname{Spin}(3)</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Spin}(4)\cong\operatorname{Sp}(1)\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2)\cong\operatorname{Spin}(5)</math>. This isomorphism is exhibited by identifying <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2)</math> with the group of <math>2\times 2</math> quaternionic matrices <math>g\in M_2(\mathbb H)</math> such that <math>g^*g=I</math> where <math>g^*=\bar g^T</math> is the conjugate-transpose of <math>x</math>. The [[reduced trace]] on <math>M_2(\mathbb H)</math> is invariant under <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2)</math>-conjugation, and the space of (reduced-)trace-free <math>x\in M_2(\mathbb H)</math> such that <math>x^*=x</math> is a five-dimensional euclidean space, with quadratic form <math>\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{red}}(x^2)</math>.
* <math>\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)\cong\operatorname{Spin}_0(1,4)</math>. This isomorphism is exhibited by identifying <math>\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)</math> with the group of <math>2\times 2</math> quaternionic matrices <math>g\in M_2(\mathbb H)</math> such that <math>g^*Kg=K</math> where <math>K=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1 &0\end{bmatrix}</math> and <math>g^*=\bar g^T</math> is the conjugate-transpose of <math>x</math>. The reduced trace is invariant under <math>\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)</math>-conjugation, and the space of (reduced-)trace-free <math>x\in M_2(\mathbb H)</math> such that <math>Kx^*K=x</math> is a five-dimensional pseudo-euclidean space, with quadratic form <math>\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{red}}(x^2)</math>, of signature <math>(1,4)</math>.
* <math>\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})\cong\operatorname{Spin}_0(2,3)</math>. Identify <math>\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})</math> as the subset of the ring <math>M_4(\mathbb{R})</math> of <math>4\times 4</math> real matrices <math>g</math> such that <math>gJg^T = J</math> where <math>J=\begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{bmatrix}</math> (with <math>2\times 2</math> blocks, and <math>I</math> the <math>2\times 2</math> identity matrix). The subspace <math>V\subset M_4(\mathbb{R})</math> consisting of the trace-free matrices <math>J</math> such that <math>x = -Jx^TJ</math> is five-dimensional, and the trace form defines a signature <math>(2,3)</math> pseudo-euclidean metric on it, which is preserved by the action <math>x\mapsto gxg^{-1}</math> of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})</math>.

==Physical significance==
===Classical mechanics===
The real symplectic group <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> arises in [[Hamiltonian mechanics]] as the group of linear [[canonical transformation]]s of phase space. In canonical coordinates
:<math>(q^1,\dots,q^n,p_1,\dots,p_n),</math>
its elements are precisely the linear changes of variables that preserve the standard symplectic form, or equivalently the [[Poisson bracket]].

The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math> is naturally identified with quadratic Hamiltonians on phase space: if
:<math>H(z)=\tfrac12 z^\mathrm{T}Kz,</math>
then the corresponding Hamiltonian flow is linear and defines a one-parameter subgroup of <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math>. In this sense, the symplectic group is generated by quadratic Hamiltonians.

===Quantum mechanics and the metaplectic group===
{{main|metaplectic group}}
The symplectic group acts by linear changes of coordinates in the phase space of classical mechanics. When one tries to make the same transformations act on the [[wavefunction]]s of [[quantum mechanics]], there is a phase ambiguity, and it is necessary to pass to a [[covering group|double cover]]. The [[metaplectic group]] is a double cover of the symplectic group over <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. (It has analogues over other [[local field]]s, [[finite field]]s, and [[adele ring]]s.)
